modules.title: Relations, keys & normalization
modules.description: Understand relational modeling, keys, normalization, indexes, and transactions.

lessons.title: Relations & integrity constraints
lessons.body:
### Model facts, not screens
A relation represents facts about a type of entity or relationship. A primary key identifies a row. A foreign key connects a row to a referenced key.

### Decide what must remain true
Use uniqueness, required values, and references to express integrity rules. A surrogate ID does not automatically make an email address unique. If uniqueness is a business rule, represent it explicitly.

### Think about cardinality
One customer can place many orders. Each order belongs to one customer. Put the customer reference on the order.

lessons.title: Dependencies & normalization
lessons.body:
### Notice repeated facts
If every order stores a customer name and email, changing the email may require many updates. A failed update can leave conflicting copies.

### Separate independent facts
Keep customer attributes in Customers and order attributes in Orders. Connect them using a customer key. Split order line items into a separate relation when one order contains many products.

Normalization is driven by dependencies, not by splitting every table as much as possible. Denormalization is a deliberate tradeoff that needs an update strategy.

exercises.title: Model customers and orders
exercises.prompt: A spreadsheet has order_id, customer_email, customer_name, product_id, product_name, quantity, and unit_price. An order can contain multiple products. Design tables and keys that avoid repeating customer and product names on each line. Explain how to preserve the price actually paid.
hints: Separate Customers, Orders, Products, and OrderItems.
The order-item key can combine order_id and product_id if a product appears only once per order.
Historical unit price belongs on the order item.
exercises.answer: Use Customers(customer_id, email UNIQUE, name), Orders(order_id, customer_id FK), Products(product_id, name), and OrderItems(order_id FK, product_id FK, quantity, unit_price_at_purchase). Choose an explicit line_id when a product can appear on multiple lines. Store the purchase price on the line so later price changes do not rewrite order history.
